overview:
Oman sits on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, with long coasts on the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and borders with the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Yemen. At about 310,000 km² it is roughly the size of Poland, and much of it is desert, gravel plain and bare mountain.

About 5 million people live in Oman, and Arabic is the official language, though English is widely used in business and schools. Muscat, the capital, is a low white city squeezed between dark mountains and the sea, guarded by Portuguese-built forts and famous for its grand mosque and opera house.

Oman is a monarchy ruled by a sultan, with an appointed council and a partly elected consultative assembly. Oil and gas pay for much of the country, but Oman is also known for dates, fish, copper and frankincense, the fragrant tree resin that made its southern coast rich thousands of years ago.
landAndNature: The Hajar Mountains curve along the north, rising to Jebel Shams at about 3,000 meters above a canyon so deep it is nicknamed Oman's Grand Canyon. Between the peaks, villages grow pomegranates and roses on terraces watered by falaj channels, ancient stone canals that carry mountain water for kilometers by gravity alone. Inland lies the Rub al Khali, the Empty Quarter, one of the largest sand deserts on Earth, and the Wahiba Sands, where dunes run in long orange ridges. The southern region of Dhofar catches the Indian Ocean monsoon each summer, turning its hills startlingly green. Wadis hold clear pools year-round, Arabian oryx roam protected reserves, and thousands of green turtles nest on the beach at Ras al Jinz.
peopleAndCulture: Omanis are known for quiet hospitality: guests are greeted with dates and cardamom coffee poured from a long-spouted pot called a dallah. Men often wear a white dishdasha robe and a kuma cap or a wrapped turban, and many carry a curved dagger, the khanjar, which appears on the national flag. Shuwa, meat spiced and wrapped in leaves then buried in a hot pit for a day or more, is the great feast dish. Camel racing and bullfighting without killing, where two bulls push head to head, are traditional entertainments, and soccer is the modern favorite. Omani sailors were legendary navigators, and their dhows carried goods to India, Africa and China.
history: Copper from Oman was traded to Mesopotamia more than 4,000 years ago, when the region may have been the land Sumerians called Magan. Frankincense from Dhofar traveled by camel caravan and ship to Egypt, Greece and Rome. Islam arrived in the 600s during the Prophet Muhammad's lifetime, and most Omanis follow the Ibadi branch. Portugal seized Muscat in 1507 and held it until Omani forces drove them out in 1650. Oman then built a maritime empire of its own, taking Zanzibar and stretches of the East African coast; for a time the sultan ruled from Zanzibar rather than Muscat. Britain gained strong influence in the 1800s. In 1970 Sultan Qaboos took power from his father and used oil income to build schools, hospitals and roads across a country that had almost none.
funFacts: Oman's falaj irrigation channels have carried mountain water to farms for about 2,000 years, and some are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
The Dhofar region turns green each summer when monsoon clouds sweep in, while the rest of Arabia bakes.
Frankincense trees grow wild in Oman, and their dried sap once traded for roughly its weight in gold.
Oman ruled the island of Zanzibar off Africa, and for part of the 1800s its sultan lived there instead of in Muscat.
Thousands of green sea turtles crawl ashore each year at Ras al Jinz, one of the largest nesting sites in the Indian Ocean.
